pass_a_gloss: Their nature burns brighter than visible things; limbs like sapphire, faces darker than ash. Those set apart for God—called Nazirites, as Symmachus and Theodotion translate the holy in Amos—Moses recalls, like Samson. Known among Jews, their purity tried by snow, their light by milk; yet tested by asceticism in what they vowed to God. The chosen among them—shown by the fragment—hold heavenly citizenship, sapphire-hued. They also bear golden veins, Symmachus showing their constitution as incorruptible and fire-enduring in godliness. Having fallen from spiritual light, weakened by mental famine, they are like dry wood, unplanted by streams—such are their priests now, lacking spiritual food. By the clear word, their faces blackened from extreme shame, for though sinning like all, they were led astray; even now, the disgraced are named thus. Better to die quickly in war than waste from hunger due to barren fields. One could call the sword and dagger God’s word—Paul says: “the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God”—by whom, Bride declares love’s wound. David urges sword at thigh, glory and beauty. Those pierced by such blades fall under Jesus’ feet—“nations shall fall beneath you”—having sworn allegiance, not starved spiritually. Christ, Bethlehem-born, is land’s fruit, “House of Bread”; Jews, unfed, fled to demon realms. Lord’s blessed field, richly scented, Jacob-winded, shows Christ’s Church. 105 Lest women seem child-eaters via cruelty, he calls them pitiful, yet ties it to famine’s force. Igniting and roasting shows Roman siege; thus total ruin he terms shattering. In Lamentations two, he frames present anguish as sorrow’s stuff. Josephus precisely logged this and other pains in siege chronicles. 106 Post-Christ advent, these ended. 107 Maybe site strength, walls, garrison power—but chiefly, God’s constant city guard. Still, pre-Nebuchadnezzar, Egyptians repeatedly seized Lord’s house treasures, spared city razing; not fiercely pressing, though foe. Origen says earthly rulers and demonic forces acted against God and Christ in ignorance; if they had known the Lord of glory, they would not have crucified Him. They thought Jerusalem would not fall, trusting in the patriarchs’ promise, unaware of Christ’s mystery. The Savior’s just blood, fully shed, destroyed those who poured it out, even as they tried to balance guilt by prophetic blood. Symmachus says they became deranged, blind in their paths, drenched in blood so they could not touch their clothes. Scripture calls angels “watchers,” as in Daniel; maybe the Mosaic law came through angels, as hinted by “if the law given by angels…” Those holding to the law and temple, though shaken, were later removed. Josephus notes priests entering the temple as usual for worship first felt movement, then heard a loud shout.
pass_b_english:
More fiery in nature than the things visible to the eye, sapphire are their limbs, their appearance darker than soot. Those who sanctified themselves to God, he says, are made holy—indeed, the term Nazirites conveys this, as Symmachus and Theodotion likewise rendered the sanctified in Amos as Nazirites. Moses also remembers these, of what sort he was, and even Samson. They were also prominent among the Judeans. Therefore, their purity was tested against snow, their brightness against milk; yet they were refined by ascetic discipline, having been proven in what they had promised to God. But the elect among them—this is indicated by the fragment—possess a heavenly commonwealth, for such is the color of sapphire. Moreover, they have golden veins, by which Symmachus represents their constitution, possessing incorruptibility and enduring fire through piety. From the spiritual radiance they have fallen, weakened by intellectual hunger, so as to resemble dry wood, like those not planted by the watercourses; such are now the priests among them, possessing no spiritual nourishment. And according to the explicit statement, their faces have grown blackened from utter shame, because, though sinning like others, they were led away; and even now, the custom among those being disgraced is to use the name in this way. For in war, it is better to die swiftly than to be subdued by famine due to lack of field produce. One might even say the sword and the dagger are the word of God—for Paul says: “and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God”—by whom,

The bride says, "I am wounded by love." And David also says, "Gird your sword upon your thigh, mighty one, in your splendor and your beauty." Those struck by such swords—spears of divine judgment—it is fitting that they fall beneath Jesus’ feet, as it is written: "The peoples shall fall under you." They have confessed his kingdom, yet they are not to be destroyed by spiritual famine. For Christ is the offspring of a land, he who was born in Bethlehem, which is called "House of Bread." The Jews, having become estranged from this bread, have been driven away into the land of demons. But the field blessed by the Lord, exceedingly fragrant, which Jacob breathed upon, signifies the Church of Christ. 105 Lest the women think they have eaten their children through cruelty, he says they are compassionate; yet he attributes this to the necessity of scarcity. The act of kindling and roasting indicates what came to pass during the Roman siege; therefore, he calls the complete destruction of the nation a shattering. And in the second chapter of Lamentations, he treats the present suffering as an element of sorrow. And this, along with all other passions, Josephus has transmitted with accuracy in his writings on the siege. 106 For after the coming of Christ, these things were completed. 107 Perhaps indeed because of the strength of the place, the fortress, and the strength of its inhabitants, but most of all because of the God who continually protects the city. Yet before Nebuchadnezzar entered, the Egyptian often took the treasures from the house of the Lord, but did not destroy the city; for he did not greatly oppress it, even if he was an enemy.

Origen reflects on the paradoxical nature of divine wisdom, noting how the rulers of the earth and the demonic powers that once governed the nations—those referenced in Scripture as having gathered together against the Lord and His Christ—acted in ignorance. Had they understood the true identity of the Lord of glory, they would not have crucified Him. Their lack of knowledge stemmed from a mistaken belief that Jerusalem would not ultimately fall, as they clung to the idea that God’s promise to the patriarchs would be fulfilled in their time, unaware of the deeper mystery surrounding Christ. Yet it is precisely the righteous blood of Christ the Savior, poured out completely, that those who shed it ultimately destroyed themselves, even as they attempted to find moderation by comparing their guilt to the blood of the prophets. Symmachus describes the aftermath: they became unstable, blind in their ways, covered in blood to such an extent that they could not even touch their own garments. Meanwhile, Scripture calls the angels “watchers,” as seen in Daniel, and it is possible that the law given through Moses was mediated by such beings, as suggested by the phrase “if the law spoken through angels was…” Those who persisted in clinging to the law and the temple, despite being shaken by these events, were eventually displaced. Josephus records that when the priests approached the temple as was their custom for the sacrificial rites, they first reported sensing a movement, and then suddenly heard a loud voice—
